intro: In the spring of 1520 a fleet under Pánfilo de Narváez reached the Gulf coast of Mexico, sent from Cuba to arrest Hernán Cortés. Spanish chroniclers later said that a man aboard one of those ships was ill with smallpox, and that the disease, never seen before on the mainland, began at Cempoala and travelled inland. By the late summer and autumn of 1520, after the Spaniards had been driven out of Tenochtitlan, it reached the Mexica capital and its neighbours. Among those it killed were Cuitláhuac, the ruler who had led the expulsion, and the Tlaxcalan lord Maxixcatzin, Cortés's ally. When the Spaniards and their Indigenous allies besieged the island city in 1521, they fought a population that had just lived through a great epidemic. Almost nothing here is a diary. The honest record is made of letters written for a king, Nahuatl annals kept by year, encyclopaedic histories compiled from the testimony of elders, and Spanish chronicles written decades later by men who had been there and by men who had not. The Nahua accounts that survive were written down after the conquest, in the Latin alphabet, often under Franciscan direction; the Spanish accounts were written to win favour, defend reputations or argue a theology. Each eye is labelled with its form and its distance in time from the events. Laid side by side, they show a striking split. The Nahua annals and Sahagún's informants put the sickness at the centre of 1520: its months, its sixty days, the people who could not move, the hunger in households where everyone lay ill, the faces left pitted, the ruler who died. Cortés, writing to Charles V on 30 October 1520 while the epidemic was at its height, says nothing of it; in his next letter, of May 1522, it occupies a few lines. The Spanish chroniclers who did tell the story fixed it on a single man, an enslaved African in Narváez's company, whose name later tradition gives as Francisco de Eguía or Baguía. That attribution is secondhand, repeated from writer to writer, and is treated here as a contested story, not a fact. How many died is unknowable with precision. Motolinía wrote that in most provinces more than half the people died (in the version printed as his Historia) or that in some provinces half died (in his Memoriales); the conquistador Bernardino Vázquez de Tapia wrote of more than a quarter. Modern scholars have defended estimates across a wide range: some once argued for an attack milder than the chroniclers claimed, while the historical demographer Robert McCaa argued in 1995 that the toll lay somewhere between a tenth and a half of the population, perhaps near the middle. The 1520 epidemic was also the first of several: later witnesses, Sahagún among them, judged the cocoliztli of 1545 and 1576 even deadlier. The numbers below are each witness's own, with whose count it is. The mass death of 1520 changed the course of the war, but no account here treats it only as a military fact. title: The Speckled Monster and the Scar on Onesimus's Arm
eyes: The six Newgate prisoners: Mary North, Ann Tompion, Elizabeth Harrison, John Alcock, John Cawthery, Richard Evans
places: His house and shop near Dock Square, Boston; London 1724–26
His house in Boston, near the Town House
His house in the North End of Boston
James Franklin's printing house, Queen Street, Boston
intro: Smallpox came back to Boston in the spring of 1721 after nineteen years away, probably with the ship Seahorse from the West Indies. By the following February about 5,800 people, more than half the town, had caught it, and about 844 had died. In the same months, a few physicians on both sides of the Atlantic tried something that most of their colleagues considered reckless: deliberately giving healthy people smallpox through a cut in the skin, in the hope of a milder disease and lifelong protection. The knowledge did not come from European medicine. In Boston, Cotton Mather learned it from Onesimus, a West African man enslaved in his household, who showed him the scar of the operation; Mather also read the reports of Timoni and Pylarini from Constantinople. In Turkey, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu watched the practice and had her son inoculated. Onesimus left no account of his own, and nor did Jack and his little son Jackey, whom Zabdiel Boylston inoculated with his own son on 26 June 1721, or the six condemned prisoners whom Charles Maitland inoculated at Newgate that August in return for their lives. They are given eyes here and flagged as known only through others. The record is mostly not diaries. Mather's and Samuel Sewall's diaries are set beside newspaper letters, pamphlets, a surgeon's case book, a letter of invitation, edited embassy letters and statistical papers, and each is tagged by form. Boston's argument was fought in print: the Boston News-Letter, the Boston Gazette, and from August 1721 James Franklin's New-England Courant, where the young Benjamin Franklin was an apprentice. The two sides argued both medicine and religion. Opponents such as the physician William Douglass said the method was untried, spread infection and was the clergy's business only by usurpation; others said that to give a disease on purpose was to defy God. Supporters said that Providence had shown a means of safety and that refusing it was the real presumption. London ran a parallel experiment by other means: royal patronage, invited witnesses, trials on prisoners and parish orphans, and then the inoculation of two princesses in April 1722. James Jurin, Secretary of the Royal Society, then turned the argument into numbers, comparing deaths after natural and after inoculated smallpox, and Boylston's Boston table entered his reckoning. Later evidence confirmed that inoculation greatly reduced the individual's risk of death but could spread smallpox to others, which is why it was eventually replaced by vaccination. Both of those points were made in 1721 by people who disagreed bitterly with each other.

intro: In late August 1793 a fever began killing people along the Water Street wharves of Philadelphia, then the capital of the United States and its largest city, with about 50,000 people. By the time cold weather ended it in November, Mathew Carey had counted 4,041 named dead; later estimates put the toll near 5,000, roughly one resident in ten. About a third of the city fled, the President among them. The federal government dispersed, the banks closed, and a mayor with a committee of volunteers kept the city running. Almost none of the record is a diary. The heart of this chapter is a run of more than fifty letters Benjamin Rush wrote to his wife, nearly every day, from the city's busiest sickrooms, printed in 1892. Around them stand dated letters by Jefferson, Hamilton and Washington; a Quaker matron's diary of names; a Lutheran pastor's account built from his journal; the committee's minutes; and four printed accounts written in the aftermath by Carey, Rush, the refugee physician Jean Devèze, and Absalom Jones and Richard Allen. The form tags say which is which, and Samuel Breck's recollections, written decades later, are marked as memory. The physicians did not agree on anything that mattered. Rush thought the fever was bred locally from putrid matter, perhaps a spoiled cargo of coffee, and treated it with huge purges of calomel and jalap and repeated bleeding. The College of Physicians and Carey thought it had been imported from the West Indies, where refugees from the revolution in Saint-Domingue had sailed from that summer. Devèze, who had treated the fever in the Caribbean, thought it local but not contagious, and treated it gently. Hamilton credited his recovery to a West Indian treatment of bark and cold baths, and the choice of cure took on party colours. These are given as positions. A century later the mosquito Aedes aegypti was shown to carry the disease, which explains both the ships and the frost. The heaviest work fell to Black Philadelphians. Rush, wrongly believing they were largely spared, urged Jones and Allen to help; they and their community nursed, bled and buried through the worst weeks, and 305 Black people were buried that year against 67 the year before. When Carey's pamphlet accused some Black nurses of extortion and plunder, Jones and Allen answered in print with names and accounts. Nurses such as the widow Sarah Bass, and Rush's servant Marcus, who nursed him through his relapse, appear only in others' pages: no surviving firsthand account by them has been found. Read across, the eyes show the same weeks as a medical crusade, a list of neighbours' names, a divine judgment, a constitutional problem and a test of who would serve. The death counts are other people's counts, each made by a different method, and they are labelled by whose they are.

title: Arm to Arm: The Vaccine Goes Round the World
eyes: Francisco Javier de Balmis y Berenguer
places: Bocas de Ceniza, mouth of the Magdalena
New Granada, Quito, Peru, Upper Peru
aboard the María Pita and Magallanes; Caribbean, New Spain, Philippines, Macao, Canton, St Helena
aboard the María Pita and Magallanes; later Puebla, New Spain
intro: On 14 May 1796 Edward Jenner, a country surgeon in Berkeley, Gloucestershire, took matter from a cowpox sore on the hand of the dairymaid Sarah Nelmes and put it into two small cuts on the arm of James Phipps, an eight-year-old boy from a local labouring family. Six weeks later he inoculated the boy with smallpox matter, and nothing happened. Jenner had tested his idea on a child who could not consent; the book he printed in 1798, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, numbered Phipps as Case XVII among other children used the same way. The new 'vaccine' (from vacca, cow) had one great weakness: it did not keep. Dried on threads, glass or lancets it often died in transit, and over a long sea voyage it almost always did. The only reliable way to carry it was in a living body, passing it from the ripe pustule of one unvaccinated person to the next every nine or ten days. That is how it crossed oceans in this chapter: arm to arm. The Spanish crown's answer was the Royal Philanthropic Vaccine Expedition. Under a Royal Order of 1 September 1803 the military physician Francisco Javier de Balmis sailed from A Coruña on the corvette María Pita on 30 November 1803 with twenty-two boys aged about three to nine — foundlings from the orphanages of A Coruña and Santiago, plus Benito Vélez, the adopted son of the orphanage rectoress Isabel Zendal (spelled Sendales, Zendala and Gómez Sandalla in Balmis's own papers). The boys were the vaccine's container. Two at a time were vaccinated from the previous pair. They had no say. Later legs used more children: 26 Mexican boys across the Pacific to Manila, three Filipino boys to Macao, and children taken from Venezuela, Cartagena and Cuba, including enslaved children. The expedition did not arrive in a vacuum. In Puerto Rico the surgeon Francisco Oller had been vaccinating for weeks with lymph from the Danish island of St Thomas; in Havana Tomás Romay had already begun; in Mexico the viceroy disputed Balmis's numbers; in Macao a Portuguese trader's crew had brought the vaccine from Manila before Balmis did, and the East India Company surgeon Alexander Pearson and his Chinese pupil Qiu Xi were spreading it in Canton. By other roads it had reached Boston (Benjamin Waterhouse, 1800), Thomas Jefferson's Monticello (1801) and Bombay (1802), where a three-year-old girl, Anna Dusthall, became the source of much of India's vaccine. The record is mostly letters, official reports, lists and treatises rather than diaries, and it is uneven. Physicians and officials wrote; the children who carried the vaccine, and Isabel Zendal who nursed them, left no surviving firsthand accounts — they appear only in other people's lists and letters, and this chapter says so wherever they appear. Disputes about priority (who vaccinated first, whose lymph was genuine) and about whether cowpox protected at all are given as the positions people held at the time. title: King Cholera Crosses the World
eyes: New York City Board of Health (institution)

Aboard the brig Laurel on the St Lawrence; Montreal; then Cobourg
Bolshoye Boldino, Nizhny Novgorod province, cut off from Moscow by quarantine cordons

intro: Cholera had spread out of Bengal in 1817. In the late summer of 1830 it reached Moscow, and over the next two years it crossed the Russian Empire, the Baltic, Britain, France and the Atlantic. This chapter follows one disease along that road on one timeline: Moscow and the Russian cordons in 1830, the St Petersburg riots of 1831, Sunderland in October 1831, London in February 1832, Paris in March and April, Quebec and Montreal in June, New York from late June to the autumn. No one at the time knew what caused it. Contagionists held that it passed from person to person and called for quarantines, cordons and isolation hospitals; anticontagionists blamed foul air and local filth and pointed to the harm cordons did to trade and the poor. Both positions are recorded here as the witnesses held them. The evidence that cholera spreads chiefly through contaminated water came later, from 1849 to the 1880s. The record is uneven, and the chapter says so. Pushkin's letters show the epidemic as quarantine and distance; Greville's diary shows the government's desk, where every order had a cost in trade. Heine reported from inside Paris in its worst weeks, when the prime minister Casimir Perier fell ill (he died on 16 May) and the funeral of General Lamarque, another victim, set off the rising of 5–6 June. In Leith, Thomas Latta tried something new: large injections of salt solution into the veins of the dying, following O'Shaughnessy's analysis of their blood. Months later the same treatment was being tried in a Devon village whose parson kept a diary. Across the Atlantic the disease came with emigrant ships through the new quarantine station at Grosse Île. Two English sisters, Catharine Parr Traill and Susanna Moodie, passed it that summer; Traill caught cholera in Montreal and recovered. In New York the merchant Philip Hone watched the news come south, and an ordinary letter-writer described crowds reading the Board of Health's daily count. Several eyes here are institutions (the London Central Board of Health and the New York Board of Health), known through their orders and posted returns, and one is an emperor known largely through other people's memoirs. The poorest victims, among them the Irish poor of London's riverside, the emigrants at Grosse Île and the rioters of St Petersburg, left no firsthand writing that has been found; they appear through others' records, which often blamed them.

intro: In the night between 31 August and 1 September 1854 cholera broke out in the streets around Broad Street, Soho, with a speed nobody in London had seen. John Snow, who lived a few streets away, counted upwards of five hundred fatal attacks within about 250 yards in ten days; his day-by-day table runs to 616 deaths between 19 August and 30 September. Three quarters of the residents fled within a week. The handle of the street pump was removed on 8 September, and the outbreak, already falling, ended. The outbreak is famous now as the moment the water theory was proved, but the record shows something slower and more contested. In 1854–55 most physicians and officials held that cholera rose from a local atmosphere fouled by sewers, filth and crowding, acting on bodies weakened by poverty or fear. Snow held that it passed in swallowed matter from the sick, mainly through drinking water. Both were positions with evidence. The national General Board of Health's committee weighed his Broad Street case and rejected it; the parish's own inquiry, by a single casting vote, endorsed it. The organism itself, seen under the microscope by Pacini in Italy in 1854, would not be widely accepted as the cause until after Koch's work in 1883–84. The honest record here is mostly letters to journals, official returns, inspectors' reports and a parish inquiry, not diaries; their dates are firm, and most are in public-domain print. They are laid out here as a case file: the physician who mapped the deaths, the curate who tried to prove him wrong, the statistician whose weekly lists both sides used, the Board's inspectors who blamed the drains, the hospital physician counting beds, a critic reviewing the evidence, and a newspaper reaching for a plague pit. Later recollections, chiefly Whitehead's from 1865 to 1874, are labelled as written later. Two households stand at the centre and left no words of their own. At 40 Broad Street, five-month-old Frances Lewis fell ill on 28 August and died on 2 September; her father, a police constable, fell ill on the day the pump was closed and died eleven days later. Her mother's account of washing the napkins survives only in the curate's report. In Hampstead, Susannah Eley, who had water carted from the Broad Street pump because she liked its taste, died on 2 September. They are given eyes so that the arithmetic has names; what they felt is not recorded.

intro: In September 1854 an allied army of British, French and Ottoman troops landed in the Crimea to besiege the Russian naval base at Sevastopol. Within weeks the war was being fought as much in hospitals as in trenches. Cholera, dysentery, scurvy, frostbite and later typhus killed far more men than shot and shell did, on every side. Wounded and sick British soldiers were shipped across the Black Sea to the vast Ottoman barracks at Scutari (Üsküdar), facing Constantinople. Russian wounded poured into improvised hospitals inside the besieged city. French sick filled the hospitals of Constantinople and the camp at Kamiesch. This chapter is built mostly from dated letters, newspaper dispatches, official reports and memoirs written soon after, not from diaries, and the form tags say so. Florence Nightingale's letters to Sidney Herbert are quoted only from their pre-1929 printing in Sir Edward Cook's Life (1913). Mary Seacole's Wonderful Adventures (1857) is a memoir written within a year of her return. Nikolai Pirogov's Sevastopol letters to his wife and Ekaterina Bakunina's memoir of the Russian Sisters of Mercy are Russian texts, given here as digests. Leo Tolstoy's sketch of the Sevastopol hospitals was written by a serving artillery officer in the spring of 1855 and is quoted from Isabel Hapgood's 1888 English translation. Nightingale and Seacole stand here on equal footing, as two women who went east by different roads. Nightingale went as a government superintendent with 38 nurses and the Times Fund behind her. Seacole, a Jamaican-born healer and businesswoman, was turned away by every office she applied to in London, sailed at her own expense and built a store and canteen two miles from Balaclava. Their reputations have been argued over ever since, sometimes as if one had to be diminished for the other to stand. The record supports neither a single heroine nor a rivalry. They met once at Scutari, briefly and civilly, and did different work in different places. Positions differ. Biographers of Nightingale, such as Lynn McDonald, stress her administration and her later sanitary and statistical work. Seacole's champions stress her independent care at the front and the prejudice she overcame. The 2016 statue of Seacole at St Thomas' Hospital revived the argument over whether she should be called a nurse or a pioneer of nursing. The entries let each woman's record speak for itself. Around them stand the people who exposed, inquired into and counted the dead. They include the Times correspondents whose October 1854 reports set off the public outcry, the Director-General who denied it, the parliamentary committee that brought down a government, and the Sanitary Commission that flushed the drains of Scutari. Also here are a French army medical inspector, a French chef who rebuilt the hospital kitchens, and a Scottish bishop's daughter who nursed in the Barrack Hospital. title: The Searchers at the Door: Plague in Bombay and Poona
places: Bombay and other plague centres, then London
General Plague Hospital and segregation camps, Poona
Mandvi and the municipal offices, Bombay
Plague laboratory at Grant Medical College / J. J. Hospital and Byculla jail, Bombay

intro: In August and September 1896 the weekly death returns of Bombay crept above their five-year averages, and fevers with swollen glands were being treated quietly in the crowded grain-dealers' quarter of Mandvi, near the docks. On 23 September a Goan private practitioner, Acácio Gabriel Viegas, said publicly what the returns implied: the disease was bubonic plague, the same illness Alexandre Yersin had isolated in Hong Kong two years before. Within months it had reached Poona, Karachi and much of western India; by the official count it would kill millions across the subcontinent over the next two decades. The response set colonial power against the household. The Epidemic Diseases Act received the Governor-General's assent on 4 February 1897 and allowed officials to inspect houses, remove the sick to hospitals, hold contacts in segregation camps, search railway passengers and destroy property. In Bombay a Plague Committee under General W. F. Gatacre and in Poona a Special Plague Committee under W. C. Rand of the Indian Civil Service used soldiers, British and Indian, in house-to-house search parties. Officials recorded falling death counts and orderly procedure; the people searched, and the Marathi and Anglo-Indian press that spoke for some of them, recorded intrusion into kitchens and shrines, the exposure of women, burned belongings and families taken to camps. Both positions are given here in their own records. Officials investigating the complaints in 1897 reported them as unsubstantiated; the complainants and their newspapers did not accept that finding. Fear also emptied the city. According to the Sanitary Commissioner's figures, roughly 400,000 people, a little under half of Bombay's population, had left by the end of January 1897; mills ran a fraction of their machinery, and on 29 October 1896 millworkers stoned the Arthur Road infectious diseases hospital in protest against forced removal. No firsthand account by a millworker has been found for this chapter; they appear in the records of employers, inspectors and newspapers. The same is true of Savitribai Phule, the Poona teacher and reformer who died on 10 March 1897 after nursing plague patients: no surviving firsthand account of her plague work was found. Medicine moved fast. Waldemar Haffkine, a Russian-born bacteriologist sent from Calcutta, made a killed-culture vaccine in a makeshift laboratory, injected himself on 10 January 1897, and three weeks later inoculated volunteers among the prisoners of the Byculla House of Correction during an outbreak there. The record names none of those prisoners; they survive only as counts. In June 1898, in Karachi, Paul-Louis Simond of the Institut Pasteur showed in a rough experiment that plague passed between rats through their fleas, a finding doubted for years before it was confirmed. title: The Three-Day Fever That Was Not

intro: In the autumn of 1918 a disease most doctors had thought of as an unpleasant three-day fever killed, within about twelve weeks, more people than the four years of war then ending. Estimates made long afterwards run from about 17 million to 50 million or more deaths worldwide, with India alone losing somewhere between 12 and 18 million. Unusually, it killed young adults in their twenties and thirties, the age of soldiers, mineworkers and new parents. Very few of the people in this chapter kept diaries. The honest record of 1918 is mostly letters, official notices, death returns and the reports of inquiries, and the form tags say so. A Kansas doctor's few printed lines, a ward physician's letter from Camp Devens, a painter's note from Vienna and a poet's memoir from the Ganga are set beside city health officers in Philadelphia and Bombay, the US Surgeon General's circular, and the inquiries that New Zealand, South Africa and Britain held when it was over. Several of these voices were first printed long after 1918, and their entries are digests. The timeline has three waves. A milder one in spring and early summer 1918 was noticed in American army camps, in Spain, whose uncensored press gave the pandemic its misleading name, and in Bombay's docks. The deadly second wave from September to December swept from the camps of Massachusetts and the troopships off Africa to Philadelphia, Kimberley, Bombay, Vienna and, carried by a single steamer, Western Samoa. A third wave in early 1919 killed, among others, Brazil's president-elect Rodrigues Alves, who died in Rio de Janeiro on 16 January 1919 without taking office. The doctors of 1918 did not know what they were fighting. The leading theory named a bacterium, Pfeiffer's bacillus, found in the throats of many patients; the US Public Health Service taught it, and vaccines were made from it. Experiments on volunteers from a naval detention camp in Boston Harbor failed to transmit the disease at all, and by 1920 the British report called the bacillus unproven and a filter-passing virus possible. Later evidence settled the question: the human influenza virus was isolated in 1933, and the 1918 virus, an H1N1 strain, was sequenced from preserved tissue and reconstructed in 2005. Most deaths, it is now understood, came from bacterial pneumonias following the viral infection, which no medicine of 1918 could cure. The numbers in these pages were recorded by people who were frightened, exhausted, grieving or defending their decisions. Where a count belongs to a city, an army or an inquiry, the ledger says whose it is. Where the dead were colonised workers in compounds or villagers on a riverbank, the record is thinnest exactly where the losses were greatest.

intro: In 1952 the United States reported 57,879 cases of polio, the worst year it had known. Most of the paralysed were children, and every summer parents closed swimming pools and kept children home. That year, in Pittsburgh, Jonas Salk began injecting a killed-virus vaccine into children at two Pennsylvania institutions: the D. T. Watson Home, whose young residents had already been paralysed by polio, and the Polk State School, whose residents had intellectual disabilities and were wards of the state, consented for by officials. Those children left no words of their own that have been found; they appear here only in Salk's numbers. Three years later, on 12 April 1955, Thomas Francis Jr. stood up in Ann Arbor and reported that the vaccine worked. Between those dates came the largest medical trial yet attempted: some 1.8 million 'Polio Pioneers', paid for by the dimes and door-to-door marches of the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis under Basil O'Connor. The first was a six-year-old in McLean, Virginia, on 26 April 1954. The trial was also a fight over method. Francis would evaluate it only if part of it used an injected placebo; the Foundation and most states preferred simply to watch unvaccinated classmates; Albert Sabin thought there should be no trial yet. The compromise ran both designs at once. The record for this chapter is almost entirely official, institutional and press material, not diaries: published papers, foundation announcements, a university press release, presidential remarks, cabinet minutes, surveillance reports marked for official use only, and newspaper interviews. The form tags say so. Because all of it is twentieth-century material, entries are digests, quoting only US-government records and a few world-famous phrases. The licences were signed the afternoon of the report. Two weeks later children vaccinated with lots from Cutter Laboratories in Berkeley began to fall ill, and by 7 May the Surgeon General, Leonard Scheele, had stopped the national programme. The Communicable Disease Center's new surveillance unit counted every case and showed a common source. Bernice Eddy, an NIH scientist, had found paralysed monkeys in her tests of Cutter lots months earlier, according to later accounts. Canada, using only Connaught vaccine, kept vaccinating. Blame for Cutter is laid out here as positions. The government's own investigators pointed at Cutter's production and at testing standards that allowed live virus through. Critics in Congress blamed Oveta Culp Hobby's department and the haste of licensing. Sabin argued the killed vaccine was unsafe in principle, while Salk and O'Connor held that one maker's failure had been allowed to discredit a sound vaccine. A California jury in 1958 found Cutter liable without finding it negligent. By the end of 1955 the programme had resumed under tighter rules, and polio cases in the United States fell by half the next year.
